text: Sources describe limited durability of cueing effects: the APTA guideline states that the lasting effects of cueing are unclear because benefits appear to dissipate over time, and that effects appear to dissipate when the cues are removed; the RESCUE crossover trial (153 patients; 3-week home cueing programme using a prototype cueing device) reported that effects of intervention had reduced considerably at 6-week follow-up; and a narrative review of cueing in people with freezing of gait reported that long-term consolidation and transfer of the effects appear to be hampered in that subgroup. (high confidence)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017; its overview page records 'Last reviewed: 19 December 2024') includes recommendation 1.7.6, 'Offer Parkinson's disease-specific occupational therapy for people who are having difficulties with activities of daily living', and recommendation 1.7.5, which advises considering referral of people in the early stages of Parkinson's disease to an occupational therapist with experience of Parkinson's disease for assessment, education and advice on motor and non-motor symptoms; the 2022 American Occupational Therapy Association practice guideline states that 'Multidisciplinary, tailored, goal-oriented intervention is recommended for people with PD'. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: In the OTiP multicentre, assessor-masked randomised controlled trial, 191 patients with Parkinson's disease and self-reported difficulties in daily activities were randomly assigned to 10 weeks of home-based occupational therapy (n=124) or usual care with no occupational therapy (n=67); the adjusted mean difference in Canadian Occupational Performance Measure score at 3 months was in favour of the intervention group (1·2; 95% CI 0·8-1·6; p<0·0001), and there were no adverse events associated with the study. (medium confidence)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: In the PD REHAB multicenter, open-label, parallel group, controlled efficacy trial, 762 patients with mild to moderate Parkinson's disease and limitations in activities of daily living were randomized to physiotherapy and occupational therapy or no therapy; there was no difference between groups at 3 months in the primary outcome, the Nottingham Extended Activities of Daily Living scale total score (difference, 0.5 points; 95% CI, -0.7 to 1.7; P = .41), the median therapist contact time was 4 visits of 58 minutes over 8 weeks, and the authors concluded that physiotherapy and occupational therapy were not associated with immediate or medium-term clinically meaningful improvements in ADL or quality of life in mild to moderate PD. (medium confidence)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: A Cochrane review of occupational therapy for Parkinson's disease, with electronic searches up to April 2007, identified two trials with 84 patients in total, and its authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support or refute the efficacy of occupational therapy in Parkinson's disease; the PD REHAB report describes Cochrane reviews of physiotherapy and occupational therapy for Parkinson's disease as having found insufficient evidence of effectiveness. (medium confidence)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: Three systematic reviews of occupational therapy-related interventions in Parkinson's disease report beneficial findings, with their authors also noting limits on the evidence base: the first (10 studies; 1343 people with Parkinson's disease and 180 caregivers) reported that interventions focussing on meaningful activities were shown to improve perceived occupational performance, and noted that few studies have identified the effectiveness of occupational therapy intervention alone; Tofani et al. (15 randomized controlled trials, 4 in the meta-analysis) reported a significant quality-of-life improvement at 2 to 3 months follow-up (mean difference of −2.08; 95% confidence interval, −2.52 to −1.64) and considered the strength of the evidence moderate because of the limited number of studies; Foster et al. (twenty-two studies) reported strong strength of evidence for physical activity levels and handwriting, moderate for IADL participation and medication adherence, and low for cognitive rehabilitation, and noted that the review is limited by the small number of studies that specifically addressed IADL function. (medium confidence)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: Three sources include cueing among their gait recommendations: the APTA clinical practice guideline states that physical therapists should implement external cueing to reduce motor disease severity and freezing of gait (FOG) and to improve gait outcomes in individuals with Parkinson disease (evidence quality: high; recommendation strength: strong), with aggregate evidence of thirteen high-quality and 16 moderate-quality studies; Keus et al. extracted cueing strategies to improve gait as one of four treatment recommendations based on evidence from more than two controlled trials; and a 2020 systematic review of physical therapy for FOG and gait impairments reports that cueing strategies (visual and auditory) reduce FOG with a good category A recommendation. (high confidence)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: Three systematic reviews or meta-analyses report improved gait speed or velocity with auditory cueing in Parkinson's disease: a 2013 meta-analysis of cueing studies (searches up to September 2011) reported significant improvement of velocity with auditory cueing (Hedge g=.544; 95% CI, .294-.795); Ghai et al. (50 studies, 1892 participants) reported an overall positive effect on gait velocity, stride length, and a negative effect on cadence with application of auditory cueing; and Nascimento et al. (2024; ten trials involving 309 participants) reported that walking training with auditory cueing improved walking speed by 0.09 m/s (95% CI 0.02 to 0.15) more than walking training alone, which the authors describe as low-quality evidence. (medium confidence)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: Sources differ on which type of external cue performs best for gait in Parkinson's disease: a 2013 meta-analysis concluded that auditory cueing is more effective for treating gait disorders in PD, a 2026 network meta-analysis reported somatosensory and visual cues as the most effective modalities for gait velocity and stride length, and the APTA guideline states, of reductions in motor disease severity when different modes of external cueing were compared, that no one mode of external cueing is superior to another. (medium confidence)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: Two meta-analyses report improved walking speed with treadmill training in Parkinson's disease but no improvement in cadence: the Cochrane review (18 trials, 633 participants; last searched September 2014) reported improved gait speed (MD = 0.09 m/s; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.03 to 0.14; moderate quality of evidence) and that cadence did not improve (MD = 2.16 steps/minute; 95% CI -0.13 to 4.46; low quality of evidence), and a second meta-analysis (16 trials across Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis) reported improved comfortable walking velocity in Parkinson's disease (MD 0.21m/second, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.27) and that treadmill training had no effect on cadence. (high confidence)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: The APTA guideline states that physical therapists should implement gait training to reduce motor disease severity and improve stride length, gait speed, mobility, and balance in individuals with PD (evidence quality: high; recommendation strength: strong) and that there was no single gait training intervention that demonstrated greater improvement than other types of gait training; two randomized trials comparing robotic gait training with treadmill training each concluded that robotic gait training was not superior (one randomly allocated 30 patients to treadmill or Lokomat gait training and, at the 6-month follow-up, found no significant differences between the 2 groups, P = .53; Picelli et al. randomly assigned sixty patients with mild to moderate Parkinson's disease into three groups). (medium confidence)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: The APTA clinical practice guideline on physical therapist management of Parkinson disease was published in Physical Therapy (2021 Dec 28;102(4):pzab302); its page carries a correction (Phys Ther. 2022 Aug 27;102(8):pzac098) about an author's affiliation and a later Editor's Note (Physical Therapy, 2024;104:pzae031) stating that Greek and Chinese translations of the article have been provided; and the guideline states that in 5 years it will either be revised by APTA, reaffirmed, or withdrawn. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: Two randomised trials of occupational therapy-related interventions in Parkinson's disease reported different primary-outcome results at 3 months: the OTiP trial (home-based occupational therapy versus usual care) reported a result in favour of the intervention on the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure, whereas the PD REHAB trial (physiotherapy and occupational therapy versus no therapy) reported no difference between groups on the Nottingham Extended Activities of Daily Living scale; the two trials differ in intervention, comparator and primary outcome measure. (medium confidence)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: Sources differ on whether external cueing reduces freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson's disease: the APTA guideline states that physical therapists should implement external cueing to reduce FOG (evidence quality: high; recommendation strength: strong) and a 2020 systematic review concluded that visual and auditory cueing are effective interventions for FOG (evidence level A-), whereas a 2026 meta-analysis of repeated external cueing found no statistically significant reduction in FOG severity versus control and rated the certainty of evidence for all outcomes as low. (medium confidence)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

text: On technology-delivered cueing, a technological review of wearable cueing systems for freezing of gait states that novel cueing systems have been evaluated predominantly in laboratory settings, a narrative review states that the increasing use of wearable technology is allowing the cue type, cue content and dose to be adapted to individual patients, and the APTA guideline notes that the cost of utilizing technology for the external cueing source should be considered. (medium confidence)
keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
